subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on April 5, 1969, the Minister of Fisheries announced the government's intention to draw further straight base lines delimiting Canada's territorial sea and exclusive fishing zones along the east coast of Nova Scotia and the west coast of Vancouver Island and the Queen Charlotte Islands. I am pleased to announce that the Governor in Council has now issued a list of geographical co-ordinates of points from which these base lines are to be drawn.
This new series of co-ordinates will be effective upon their publication in the Canada Gazette on June 11, under the authority of the 1964 Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. That legislation created, beyond Canada's previously existing three mile territorial sea, a further nine mile zone within which Canada has exclusive jurisdiction over fisheries. At the same time the 1964 legislation empowered the government to establish along the coasts of Canada a system of straight base lines which, in the areas where they were established, would replace the sinuosities of the coast as the starting point for measuring the breadth of Canada's territorial sea and fishing zones. Such base lines may be drawn from headland to headland, from island to island and across the mouth of bays. Sea areas landward of the straight base lines have the status of internal waters of Canada.
A first series of base lines was established by the government in November 1967 for the coast of Labrador and the southern and eastern coasts of Newfoundland. Pending the conclusion of negotiations with certain European countries, the fishermen of these countries have been allowed to continue, in Canada's outer nine mile zone, the fishing activities they had been carrying out in those areas where they had traditionally fished prior to the passage of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act and the establishment of base lines thereunder.
The countries involved in these negotiations were Great Britain, Norway, Denmark,
June 4, 1969

Canadian Territorial Sea Limits France, Portugal, Spain and Italy. All of these have traditional fishing practices on Canada's east coast. It is now proposed to proceed further with the negotiations with the European countries concerned.
With respect to the United States, which has conducted traditional fishing activities off both Canada's east and west coasts, we intend to proceed with negotiations for the continuance of the present arrangement whereby Canadian and United States nationals are permitted to fish in the fishing zones of the other country on a reciprocal basis. Apart from traditional fishing practices, the United States and France also have certain treaty rights off Canada's east coast, and these rights will of course be respected.
A number of important gaps remain along Canada's east and west coasts after the establishment of the new series of base lines for Nova Scotia, Vancouver Island and the Queen Charlottes. As the Minister of Fisheries indicated in his announcement of April 5, the government intends to deal with certain of these gaps, as appropriate, after securing an amendment to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act during the next session of the house. The desired amendment will provide greater flexibility for dealing with coastal areas and will permit the Governor in Council to draw fisheries closing lines enclosing certain areas as exclusive fishing zones without extending the limits of Canada's internal water or territorial sea. At present, of course, Canada's fishing zones consist of a nine mile belt contiguous to the territorial sea, and therefore cannot be extended without at the same time extending Canada's internal waters and territorial sea by means of straight base lines.
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to table the order in council establishing the new base lines for Nova Scotia, Vancouver Island and the Queen Charlotte Islands, as well as the Canadian Hydrographic Service charts illustrating these base lines and the outer limits of Canada's territorial sea and fishing zones in the areas concerned.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the official opposition, we welcome the announcement made today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As you, sir, and the house are well aware, we have been diligently seeking this information ever since the legislation was passed away back in 1964. I am sure the fishermen on the east coast today have a better understanding of the meaning of the word 
"eternity", because they have waited from 1964 until Wednesday, June 4, 1969, for the announcement just made, which outlines some of the areas to be protected by the base lines which were outlined in the legislation of 1964.
The legislation was of course quite definite in providing that these base lines would be announced, but they are still incomplete. The minister's statement indicates that base lines, as provided in the legislation, will be drawn from headland to headland, from island to island, across the mouth of bays, and so on. I point out to the minister that if they were drawn from headland to headland on the south coast of Newfoundland, for example, they would run right into the middle of the territory of the French government in the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS
speechtext: The government doesn't care about that.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS
speechtext: No, they apparently are not applying themselves to this problem, because we heard nothing in the minister's announcement about any agreement with the French government or just what action will be taken in drawing the base lines in that area. This is a very important matter, because the common market countries have indicated that it is their intention to set up a base on the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and the expanded fishery which will flow from that base will have serious, injurious effects upon the available supplies of fish on the east coast.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING STRAIGHT BASE LINES DELIMITING CANADIAN TERRITORIAL SEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, five years is a rather long time to wait for such an insignificant and incomplete announcement because, as has always been said, the fish of the ocean are no respecters of arbitrary lines which range across the oceans without regard to the desires of the government which establishes them. As was expected, the announcement of the minister did not
June 4, 1969



deal with certain areas along our coasts, notably the west coast from which I come and the bodies of water known as Queen Charlotte Sound and Dixon Entrance; these are left open to the international exploitation of fisheries, although they are areas we would normally consider our own. We are left in the position, perhaps because we are now in the fifth year since the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was presented to parliament, where we face the prospect of other nations, notably Japan and the Soviet Union, claiming historic fishing rights in areas which are not defined as Canadian territorial waters.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
In fact, the other day another Japanese fishing boat operator was arrested, charged and fined in our courts for a violation of the 12 mile limit that exists now and that follows the convolutions of the coast. So, coupled with this, we have to have a more intensive prosecution of our jurisdiction, regardless of what form it follows.
The minister made mention, as did the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) on another occasion, of the necessity of filling in these blank spots with something called the fisheries closing lines. The reason for that was that in one area, which I know in particular, the distance involved is approximately 100 miles, which is too long a distance in international law and under international acceptance along which to draw a straight line closing off such a large body of water as are the inland waters.
To get around this difficulty of the international acceptance of this idea we are to develop something called a fisheries closing line. It seems to me that if for argument's sake the government had determined and conceived that a fisheries closing line 100 miles in length will be acceptable in international law, then the government must also accept the premise that the fisheries closing line that follows the continental shelf will likewise be acceptable, and a fisheries closing line that would follow the continental shelf would be far more valuable to Canada and her fisheries than the straight base line method we have at the moment. In fact, the Committee on Fisheries which reported to this house last Friday, May 30, made just such a recommendation, that when these fisheries closing lines are drawn they be drawn in such a way as to follow the area of the continental shelf and thus give us the fullest possible amount of protection, primarily for our bottom fish which would respect that line because the continental shelf

As member of the committee on fisheries and forestry, I must say that the minister's statement is very incomplete, but that it represents nevertheless a step toward good relations with the countries to which it refers. More than ever, I would invite the government to make use of efficient methods to keep foreign fishermen-I am now thinking of Japanese fishermen in particular-from fishing in our waters. I invite the government to do everything in its power to define once and for all our fishing zones and to make sure they are observed.

Mr. Speaker, I make no apology for rising at this time to speak against Bill C-191. In fact I think there should be 263 speeches in this house directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson with regard to the oppressive provisions in Bill C-191. This bill affects most Canadians but in particular it affects those persons within the low income group. Until last night I had difficulty in determining who has been our worst minister of finance. In fact, Miss LaMarsh, that gallant parliamentarian who has left this house, indicated in her book that it was the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), but after hearing the speech of the Minister of Finance last night I think he has overtaken the former minister of that department.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
That is hard to do.

I say that in most of these measures the Minister of Finance takes an arithmetic view toward Canadian problems and does not display any of the so-called compassion which at times he indicates.
I was rather delighted to read an article in last Saturday's Toronto Star about the Minister of Finance in which it was indicated that he was a poor boy who had made good, who had worked his way up from the ranks and is now holding one of the major portfolios in the cabinet. I cannot help but think that he has moved from the position of protecting the weak and the low income groups to the position of protecting the corporate elite.
You can probably remember, Mr. Speaker, the great speeches he made when he was a member of the opposition. In those speeches he was very persuasive, very incisive and very determined that it was necessary to bring forth certain legislation affecting some of the corporate giants in this country with respect to corporate tax holidays and incentives. But now that he sits on the other side

of the house, now that he has reached the top of the ladder, he realizes that he must protect the corporate elite.
Last night's performance was a perfect example of the colossal sham which the Minister of Finance perpetrates. In fact, neither in this bill nor in his speech last night has he done anything to help the people of western Canada to solve their agricultural programs. I see nothing in this bill to help pensioners to offset their decreased purchasing power resulting from the rising inflation from which they are suffering. I heard nothing last night, nor did I hear anything today with regard to poverty, with regard to tax reform, with regard to regional development or with regard to high interest rates and, more especially, with regard to the determined penetration of American ownership into the Canadian economy.
Bill C-191 deals in the main with two major areas. One is the social development tax of 2 per cent, and the other is the imposition of taxes on insurance companies. Those are the two main areas. Yesterday we had the pleasure of hearing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) make his usual, eloquent, persuasive speech concerning the group which the social development tax will affect most. He pointed out that it is the lower income groups that are most affected by the 2 per cent tax, and that it is an oppressive tax particularly on people who are on fixed incomes such as pensions. He pointed out the dramatic example of the government accepting a 4 per cent increase in inflation while at the same time taking a niggardly attitude by increasing the payments to old age pensioners by only 2 per cent. In other words, the government is saying to these people who contributed so much to the building of Canada that even though inflation is increasing at a rate of 4 per cent per year it will give them only 2 per cent and they must absorb the other 2 per cent themselves.
I felt last night that after the persuasive speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the minister would take immediate steps to remedy the harsh treatment of these people and in his budget speech would rescind the 2 per cent social development tax. But no, he did not. He acted in his usual stubborn and callous manner in determining priorities for the Canadian economy. He seem to think that balancing the budget is more important than looking after particular

needs of the different groups within our society.
The government has placed special emphasis on some of these measures by saying that no benefits will be given, more especially to the lower income groups, without them paying and paying in full. They should take the same attitude toward their corporate friends that they take toward the lower income groups. Then there would probably be a proper adjustment. But no, they ignore the situation and these are the results we get.
I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that two years ago the government attempted to impose a 5 per cent increase in personal income tax on Canadians, and it was only when it was defeated in the house that the Minister of Finance of that time came back with a measure that imposed a 3 per cent increase in income tax on personal income and a 3 per cent increase in corporation tax. They had no idea of imposing the 3 per cent increase in corporation tax until the 5 per cent increase in personal income tax was defeated in the house.
Last year we had the great social development tax of which the minister seems to be so proud and which came into effect at the beginning of this year. We are dealing with that tax in this measure. Last night, as I say, he had the opportunity to show that he had learned something as he climbed the ladder of success from poor boy to one of the top rungs by rescinding the social development tax, but he did not do so.
The second area of this bill deals with insurance companies. One can say without hesitation that insurance companies in this country have had an unfair advantage over the years in regard to taxation. A slight improvement is being made in this legislation, and one hopes that this is only the beginning in making the insurance companies pay their fair share of corporate taxes.
One appreciates that the government has created regulations to determine what is business income. 1 might point out that this is at variance with the late Mr. Carter's proposals, in that they are much more administratively complex in determining what is income. Up to this time the investment income of the insurance companies has not been taxed, but now they will have a 15 per cent tax imposed on their investment income.
You have heard me speak many times, Mr. Speaker, about the actions of insurance companies, and you have heard me say that they

Mr. Chairman, could the
minister clarify the differences between nonparticipating and participating policies? What does the government consider taxable income in this regard? Will it tax funds left to accumulate under participating policies? Will those moneys be taxed when the policies expire, or how is this to be done? How will that tax be levied?

Mr. Chairman, basically in enacting this legislation we have worded it so as to protect and exclude from investment income tax the income in the company's hands coming from non-participating policies, since these policies were written on the basis that there will be no participation by the individual. They are written with fixed interest rates in mind. Such policies, therefore, are to be excluded from investment tax, or from considerations with respect to investment income. With respect to participating policies, the participant usually pays a premium and participates in investment income. The Carter Commission proposed that such investment income when paid to the individual in the form of dividends ought to be accrued to his benefit and taxed then in his hands. We looked very carefully at these proposals and decided they would be unwieldy to operate because it would mean that individual records would have to be kept of all those who must pay tax. Those records would have to include amounts of cash paid or received, and so on. As an alternative we decided to levy a tax on the investment income of the corporation but to exclude certain portions of that investment income in the process. As I said, in order to protect with respect to non-participating policies written at fixed premiums and in order to protect registered policies, where policyholders need protection, our legislation has been carefully drafted. Investment income will be taxed after expenses relevant to that investment income have been deducted. Those expenses are ones the company incurs in earning the investment income and include items such as certain carrying costs, certain selling costs and part of the administrative

June 4, 1969
Income Tax Act
costs of the company. Then, when investment income is determined, it is taxed at the rate of 15 per cent which, incidentally, is about the lowest tax rate on our present tax scales.
The dividends distributed out of that investment income to policyholders are not taxable in their hands, no matter whether those dividends are distributed in cash or credited to them. They are not taxable in their hands. After dividends are deducted from investment income an amount remains from which the company deducts the balance of its operating expenses. It pays tax on this net income, as does any other corporation. This provision applies to mutual and stock companies.

Could I ask the minister to clarify something, Mr. Chairman? May I cite my own case as an example. I have a 20 pay life insurance policy which was paid up 10 or 15 years ago. Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend gave a good example. I advise him not to do what he is thinking of doing. We have not made this type of legislation retroactive. As a matter of fact, the value of the policy will be computed on the second anniversary after the date of the budget. That is, it will be two years after October 22. Any moneys accumulated under the policy to that date will be non-taxable. Even in those cases where one buys life insurance and continues that life insurance in force, there will be no tax on that money in the hands of the individual, if he holds the policy until death.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This does not affect previous policies. It only affects policies which are cashed in following the second anniversary date after October 22. Say a man buys a policy at age 50, makes payments on it until he is 65, and then decides to cash it in. If he gets an amount of money back which is greater than the cost of the policy to him, it is income in his hands. It is really interest in his hands, and that is taxable. But no one need feel that they are going to lose by keeping the policies they have.

Under present circumstances for policies held up to two years from the budget date-no. What happens in the future from that date on is that if you have insurance and you pay premiums on the insurance policy, and get dividends to offset them, you may end up with a cash surrender value ten years later that is $500 more than the policy value as determined at the two year calendar date, plus all net premiums, and if the cash surrender value is greater than those two the tax is on the difference which is realized by the individual at the particular time he cashes his policy.
To take a simpler example, if you were to start fresh now and went out and bought a policy at age 20 and held it until age 50, a policy for $10,000 face value, which is worth $7,000 at the time you cash it in, then if you had paid only $6,000 in premiums and took the cash surrender value of $7,000, the $1,000 difference would be taxable in your hands. Only the investment increment realized by the individual is taxable in his hands.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to clause 27, I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as well as other hon. members, speak of discrimination between the rich and the poor, of the unjustifiable difference in the way mil-lionnaires and poor people are treated. To my mind, this smacks of demagoguery, Mr. Chairman, because in the final analysis, the principle which inspired this legislation is simple and we have lived with it for many years. We are dealing here with insurance, no more no less, and almost all our social laws are based on that payment system.
For instance, whether an individual is rich or poor, he insures his house against fire; obviously, the insurance premium is the same.
If he insures his automobile against accidents or theft, the insurance premium is the same for the poor as for the rich.
The argument is also put forth that if old people do not have enough money to subsist, it is unjust to increase their tax burden. There is much sympathy for that argument because everyone knows the difficulties- especially in a period of economic austerity such as we are now going through-those who earn small salaries or who live on pensions can experience. But a truth remains that cannot be denied, and that is that the
Income Tax Act
government cannot pay indefinitely without getting the money somewhere.
What astonishes me, what I find illogical, in the reasoning of the members of the opposition who oppose this measure, is that day after day we hear them in this house clamour quite often for expenditures of hundreds of millions of dollars. If we were to add up the requests made in this house, they would cost the government more than a billion dollars; but seldom are solutions or new sources of revenue suggested. Indeed, when the government tries to levy a tax, there is an outcry.
I understand that theories are put forward, by the Social Credit for instance, or by the New Democratic party which would like to socialize all our business concerns and make us believe that some Santa Claus could pop up and give the country inexhaustible sources of revenue while making it possible to distribute free money to everyone. But such promises seem to me like wishful thinking because they have not been proven up to now, if we are to judge on the basis of the failure experienced by other countries which made similar attempts.
The truth is harsh but it is obvious. One gets nothing for nothing. If we want to make a present to someone, we have to pay for it. The same principle applies to the government as to the individual. Money has to come from somewhere. Some will say "Tax the rich". A few years ago, an American politician, Mr. Huey Long and the political party to which he belonged used the catchword: "Soak the rich". What is going to happen? At a given time we will end up with a greater number of poor because the rich people will not be left with enough money to invest, to create jobs for the poor. Such truth should be obvious to those at least who do not believe too much in Santa Claus, and who have gone beyond that stage.
It is true that in the context in which we live, there is a category of Canadians who would certainly require either some supplementary assistance or relief from taxes. If we want to keep on providing them with what they get already, it certainly cannot be done overnight, through some miracle. The government certainly does not give anything for nothing. They must find money somewhere.

But one must also say that as far as income tax is concerned, millionaires are certainly more taxed, proportionately speaking, than in most countries of North America and of the whole world-I am referring here to Canadian millionaires-and that they are affected in other fields if they are not in that one.
Besides, the millionaire will probably be the last one to use the free health service and in most cases will want to pay for special services, for he can afford to go to hospitals where he will be provided with nursing care night and day and he will probably have nothing to do with that method which puts everybody on an equal footing.
Such an accusation is stamped with demagoguery in these times. I believe this is no time for people having a sense of responsibility to allow situations like that to continue in Canada. On the contrary, we should now remind ourselves of the words that echoed throughout the whole world, the words of the late John Kennedy: In the time we live in, ask not what your country can do for you, but rather ask what you can do for your country, in the difficult circumstances the world is going through now.
It is true that all Canadians have to tighten their belts but it is thanks to that that the Canadian economy is so healthy as compared with that of other countries. It is because the government has had the courage to enforce austerity measures readily accepted by the great majority of Canadians who understood that this austerity spell required all of them to do their part of the job, a sacrifice they have indeed accepted as the outcome of the last elections has shown. It was the same party which went to the people after it had warned Canadians it would increase taxes and curtail profits in some sectors. I believe it is healthier for the future of a nation to warn its people that they will have to accept occasional sacrifices to prevent the economy from crumbling. We should try to avoid this complacent philosophy and refrain from telling the poor: "You are exploited, you get the same deal the rich do." All in all, this brings me back to the slogan I was quoting earlier: "Soak the rich, don't help the poor." Finally, we shall come to the point where there will no longer be any rich people but just poor people. At the limit, the government will have to take care of everybody.

I know the measure is not popular but I think that under the circumstances it is justified. It should win the support of all hon. members instead of being the target of unconsidered attacks, as it was, from such a serious man as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

We might have supported these programs had they confined expenditures to limits or amounts that could be carried through shared cost programs.
This tax as introduced in this form seems to prevent the provinces from participating in such a program. Perhaps it would be the intention to absorb this tax in a more equitable way in the tax structure in the future.

Nobody in this party suggests that millionaires or anyone else should be unfairly taxed. But in a democratic society we long

People will finally realize that words alone are powerless and that nothing much is changed by adding "development" to "social". In order to really change a situation, we should come to grips with the causes of the economic unbalance and not just toss words around. Instead of calling it a social development tax, it would simply become Social credit.

Mr. Chairman, this party began a fight against this clause many months ago, and the fight that we put up contributed in part to the defeat of the former government. The people of this country are in no mood to put up with this type of taxation. They may be overcome by lethargy for a while, but a great many of them hope that the government means what it says when it talks about a just society. However, they will only retain their hope for so long.
My colleague from Comox-Alberni has spoken of our strong objection to this measure in the ground that it imposes a ceiling of $120 on the tax no matter what the income of the taxpayer is. This flouts the entire principle of taxation according to ability to pay, and we are very much opposed to this tax on this ground.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The other ground which has been dealt with relates to the term "social development tax." My colleague from Winnipeg North Centre discussed the ramifications of that title, and I want to say a few words about it also. When certain people heard the term "social development tax" they were taken in, believing that the tax would be used for social development purposes. The Canada Welfare Council recommended, for instance, in its report of last January and in earlier reports also, that family allowances be raised. Recipients of the old age security pension have been complaining bitterly that the new so-called income supplement has added to their difficulties because they have had to pay tax on their increased income. That tax has added to their difficulties which have been brought on in large measure by rising living costs. I also wish to raise the question of veterans allowances. Many think that the money the government is raising with its social development tax ought to go toward increased allowances for veterans and their families.
May I also raise the question of how we are to protect our homes. When I put forward the idea in the house that we can protect homes

by paying wages to mothers who otherwise would have to go out to work and enable those mothers to remain at home, hon. members displayed great amusement and scorn. Nevertheless, quite a few people are looking at this proposal because they realize that it is very sound indeed. They know that if we were to pay wages to mothers and enable them to stay home instead of forcing them to go out to work and leave their children unprotected, we would be making a good social investment. Many people believed that the social development tax would be used for programs of this type.
I say that we ought to look at family allowances. We should try to raise the old age security pension, increase veterans allowances and pay wages to mothers in the home. In the previous government hon. members and even ministers were making encouraging noises and promises. They said they would support the idea of having all Canadians enjoy a minimum guaranteed annual income. Yet what has happened, Mr. Speaker? Our people now realize that the social development tax is not a social development tax. It merely imposes a greater tax burden on those in low income groups least able to bear it. It is not a social development tax. It is a social deception tax. People recognize it as such.
After the Minister of Finance said tht he hoped to have a surplus of a quarter of a billion dollars in the coming fiscal year, I could hardly believe my ears when I heard that this so-called social development tax is to remain in force. In my opinion it is a completely unjust tax. Surely the government could have raised exemption levels if it wanted to find ways of lifting the burden of taxation from some of our people. Many of our people, including those receiving veterans allowances, old age security pensions and family allowances, do not earn enough to be taxed. Clearly increased income tax exemptions would not help them. It is in this field that taxation must be made fairer. Measures other than income tax exemptions could be used to help those in the very low income group.

The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) said that the opposition members consider the government as some kind of Santa Claus handing presents to all and sundry, but I wish to point out to him that Santa Claus does not start by stealing pennies from children's piggy-banks-

-and deceiving them by making them believe that it will give them presents for social development and social progress.
That is precisely what this government does. It stole pennies from the poor by raising this tax, even before it was authorized by legislation. It robbed them to give them what? More taxes and an increase in the cost of living. In fact, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) gave no indication that things would cost less in a foreseeable future.

If I could continue in French I would, but I am afraid I cannot as yet. I am more fluent in English. One of these days, though, I will become desperate and deliver an entire speech in French and hon. members will have to put up with my grammatical mistakes and unscramble my blunders. I feel most strongly on this question and I know that no matter which language the people of this country speak, they all suffer from the same problems. I am as concerned as the Prime Minister is about the language question and I support the languages bill. Nevertheless, the government ought to bring down the cost of living. It should make those best able to pay carry the greatest burden of taxation, because that is the way to national unity. You create national disunity when you discriminate against some parts of our population. If the government wants national unity in this country it had better control rising living costs and impose greater taxes on those best able to pay. We need the official languages bill, but that bill alone will not bring unity if other problems are not dealt with. The government must act on both aspects. In the meantime something must be done about the cost of living.
When we in this party talk about the need for certain universal services and ask the government not to take the backward step of applying a means test on those social services for which we fought so hard, a great hue and cry goes up on the government side of the house. Hon. members ask, "Would you give these services to millionaires?" I say, certainly I would, but I would let the computer take back any money so spent. I would take that money back in the form of income and corporation taxes which would be based on the taxpayer's ability to pay. When some of us ask, "Why not take additional taxes from our millionaires?" the cry goes up, "No, no, a 29180-617*
thousand times no, we will not take anything from our millionaires. Our poor millionaires are groaning now under their heavy tax burden. We dare not raise their taxes."
May I refer to an article about MacMillan Bloedel, a company that operates in my part of the country, in the Monetary Times for June, 1969. The article says in part:
Giant MacMillan Bloedel Co., for example, has size (1963 sales: $584.5 million), balance (lumber, pulp, paper, packaging) and international muscle.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Though it slightly trails other west coast producers in recent earnings gains and profit margins, its first quarter net was up 39 per cent and in March, according to Chairman John V. Clyne, 67, MacMillan Bloedel had the highest operating profit in its history. The company earned $38.8 million in 1968, despite a whopping 56 per cent tax rate.
There is some money, Benson.

There is where the minister can get some. It is not the whopping 56 per cent tax rate that is important. The important thing about taxes is what you have left after taxes are paid. If with this whopping 56 per cent tax rate MacMillan Bloedel is still making the highest percentage profit in its history, then the taxes on MacMillan Bloedel are too low. I warrant that the same thing is true of a great many other corporations in Canada.
We do not want to soak the rich. We want to soak the people of this country according to what they can bear in the way of soaking. Taxation should be a way of collecting fairly and distributing fairly the cost of the goods and the services we need. The Carter Commission report, which has been pigeonholed and is gathering a lot of dust, enshrined a mighty good taxation principle, namely, fairness according to ability to pay. Sooner or later that report will have to come out of its pigeonhole. When the people of Canada realize that unfairness is going to continue they will become very upset about this legislation and other pieces of legislation like it.
I receive dozens of letters each day. I do not know what kind of letters the minister gets from his constituents, but this one that I got this morning is typical of most letters I receive. It is from a veteran and it reads in part:
What most people need is more money and it makes it hard on old age pensioners. It is hard on them when prices are out of line and the stores are raising prices every time there is the least increase in wages. But pensions don't rise. I have no idea what will happen but one thing is sure: it can't continue this way much longer.

High level commissions, boards, task forces, reviews of policy and all that sort of thing will not prevent people much longer from seeing what is happening. People must have the assistance they need.
We in this corner of the chamber make no apology for having carried on this fight so strongly. We have carried it on ever since this retrogressive step was first taken, now a couple of years ago or more. We want it labelled a regressive step. It is a deception tax. We want the minister to reverse his course and adopt the principle of taxation according to ability to pay outlined in the Carter Commission report. If he will do that he will really be flexing the muscles to good purpose that he attempted to flex last night.
You cannot fight inflation with the nickels and the dimes of old age pensioners, children and other people on social welfare assistance. If you want to fight inflation you have to collect the revenue where the revenue is and impose controls where controls are needed. If the minister will do that there will be some hope of getting some kind of just society and of retaining the people's faith in democratic government.

Mr. Chairman, it is with pleasure that I rise to say a few words on Bill C-191, and especially on the clause respecting the social development tax which should be called the antisocial tax, because it is for the citizens a burden that deprives them of purchasing power when they do not even have enough of it.
It is a deceitful tax. They have used rather familiar terms to make the people believe that it is really a tax to help society, to give it more stimulus, when it will have quite the opposite effect.
This tax deprives society of its purchasing power when it has not enough already; moreover, it will be used mostly, as the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) said, to replenish the consolidated revenue fund and to pay increased interest rates. It will be used mostly to pay the increase in the interest rate on debentures that are renewed at the higher rate.
I am wondering how this government can do everything while it has a clear majority that should enable it to help society. It does not find anything else to do but to cause trouble.
It is not by increasing interest rates and the cost of living that we will be able to check
IMrs. Maclnnis.]
inflation which is precisely due to the increased interest rate, one of the main causes of inflation.
Inflation is caused by 20 per cent of the people, while 80 per cent are in a state of deflation. And everybody is put on an equal footing. They say that inflation is created by everybody, but it is paid for by those who are in a state of deflation.
The present government is leading us into bankruptcy. It could find other sources of revenue instead of taxing the little people, the poor, instead of reducing the purchasing power of those who already do not have enough.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
A great number of people pay taxes-I say this to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote)-and are compelled, for this purpose, to borrow on a promissory note at an interest of 10 and 12 per cent from banks or credit unions. I have endorsed many promissory notes to help people get the money needed for their taxes. I, myself, have borrowed from financial institutions to pay my taxes.
The people have no money and cannot pay more taxes; yet, the government taxes increasingly. The economic imbalance is getting worse, and this creates new problems for the people.
The financiers get rich by means of exorbitant and unreasonable interest rates, since they reduce the purchasing power which should be increased as production increases. The gross national production increases-it will increase by 5 and perhaps even by 6 per cent this year-but the purchasing power of the people decreases. Now, if the gross national production increases, the personal income should also increase.
The government is doing exactly the opposite and the solutions proposed are more trouble than we ever had before. While we are in a period of full prosperity, we should build, because anything that is physically possible should be financially possible.
There are a considerable number of programs or developments that we could carry out, but on account of the austerity system, social development is being hindered and the government has the nerve to tell the people: We are imposing a social development tax. It is the most hypocritical and ignominious tax ever seen in a country.
Communist tricks, and tricks from countries behind the iron curtain are being used to make the people believe that they are

being helped, whereas, at the present time, they no longer have enough to live. Nowadays, people lack the necessities of life. Those who enjoy a decent standard of living have to borrow money at the rate of 10, 12 and even 24 per cent. The people live on borrowed money and get deeper into debt every day.
The financiers who charge interests of 10, 12 or 24 per cent get richer all the time, in order to have more money to loan the people and get them deeper into debt, in short, to reduce to nothing any progress they make from day to day. In fact, that progress, under the form of savings, goes into the pockets or the bank accounts of those who control credit, because such people have enough power to cash in on any development. They are exploiting developments for their own benefit and at the people's expense.
Let us look at the reports of the financial tycoons. They are making $1J billion or $11 billion in profits which they take from the people's pockets, from labour, from people's savings and properties. They appropriate all that to themselves. The government has no say in the matter. It is an accomplice. It only gets deeper involved in this shocking barbarity which throttles the people and deprives them of a living.
It is claimed, as I said a while ago, that people have two or three cars, but all those cars are financed by loans at 10, 15 and even 24 per cent interest. Government has nothing to say about that. There is talk of inflation while people are destitute. Has the Minister of Finance understood the meaning of the word "inflation"?
The cost of living is increasing while it should be going down, as it would if we had a government able to balance the economy. Our government is the first responsible for the rise in the cost of living with its taxes of all kinds. This is what it is doing when it should cause the cost of living to go down by lowering, for instance, the interest rate. There is some talk of fixing prices, of fixing this or that, but no mention is made of a ceiling on interest rates. Those rates are allowed to rise and they want to fix prices on the grounds that industries or businessmen are taking advantage of the people.
Tradesmen do not take undue advantage of the people. There are some exceptions, but in general, people are not exploited by industrialists but rather by finance and governments at every level.
Indeed, provincial governments are allowed to borrow money at a rate of interest of 9 or

10 per cent and the federal government refuses to interfere. They let provincial and municipal governments borrow money on foreign markets and give away our inheritance. Everything is handed over to foreigners, because the government does not want to assume its responsibilities which, after all, are not so dreadful.
The federal government could authorize the provincial governments to borrow on the basis of the administration charges instead of having them pay a 10 per cent interest as a result of which, provincial governments are deep into debt. They overtax the people and this goes beyond all logical, normal and social bounds.
Everything is bungled on account of this system. This bungling extends throughout Canada. The economy is unbalanced and the more we apply the old solutions, the more we are unbalancing our system which is on the road to ruin. And if we bankrupt the people, our governments will also be bankrupt.
They said: "We will levy taxes and the citizens will borrow at any rate of interest to pay them." Who cares. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) said a while ago: "Money does not grow on trees"; but it does not grow either in the taxpayers' pocket. Taxpayers are compelled to borrow to obtain some and then, they run into debt which they cannot repay. It is on those loans that the government is levying taxes. Taxes are levied on debts and loans and nothing else. The government could find other sources of income to finance its requirements and run the economy. The more the system will be applied, the more taxes we will have to impose, because as we go along, federal and provincial deficits get bigger.
There is an attempt to balance federal and provincial budgets by upsetting the budget of individuals. Is that a solution, Mr. Finance Minister? Tell us. Do your bills and budget contain any solution? Are there reasonable, practical proposals? No, there are not any. The proposals that are made will continue to upset the economy and increase the poverty of the people who are already more than poor, destitute, in debt up to the hilt, and already paying three times more than they can afford.
It is even impossible to pay the interests on debts. The federal government is unable to pay the interests on its debt. Individuals cannot pay the interests on their own debts, and interests on government debts, at all levels. It is impossible. That cannot work.

The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres has never understood anything about that. He says that money does not grow on trees, that we must get it from the pockets of citizens. Has the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres a formula to put money back into the pockets of taxpayers? You know how to get the money, not how to give some back. You will never find a way. I do not know why the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres cannot understand the economic situation.
I do not know whether it is from partisanship or self-interest, but he ignores the whole population, their poverty and their hardships, and he pays no heed to the forthcoming revolution which will soon be upon us because we have not kept our eyes open and have not taken up our responsibilities.
That is where we are going. The so-called social development tax should be abolished. It should be replaced by a dividend to be paid to every citizen. This would be a welcome measure, seen from another angle, if the minister were to say: A 2 per cent discount or dividend will be paid to all workers earning less than $6,000. The minister would then be commended.
Never in the history of the old parties, Grits and Tories alike, have they thought of that. And those who suggest it are considered fools, unfamiliar with logic, and walking on their head instead of on their feet.
In my opinion, those who walk on their head instead of on their feet are the two old parties that have led us to our downfall since confederation. Canada is doomed, it is on the brink of bankruptcy. As a matter of fact, the citizens, the municipalities, the provinces, everybody is on the verge of bankruptcy. This is where you have led us, dear representatives of the old parties, Liberals and Conservatives, who are applying the same solution. You never wanted to do anything else but to embarrass us and to walk upside down.

Mr. Chairman, first I should like to make a few points that I do not think have been made so far in the debate. I was both shocked and astounded last fall when the Minister of Finance brought in the so-called social development tax. I was shocked and astounded because I think it is one of the most regressive types of taxation he could possibly have introduced. It is but one example of the type of philosophy behind the government today, a government that has this

philosophy not only in the field of finance and taxation but in all other areas and jurisdictions.
I must also say that I was mildy amused but somewhat horrified by the remarks made by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres. I must say that I find it difficult to understand his position even though he may actually believe what he said. It is no wonder that many young people in our society are becoming very frustrated with the way things are going. It is no wonder they are feeling restless. They want many social and economic changes. They want equity, they want equality of opportunity, and they want some say over the way their lives are going and over the decisions that are being made in our society. So I must say I was quite appalled when I heard the member from Trois-Rivieres make some of the statements he made in the house today.
I have made the comment that the social development tax is very regressive. It is a 2 per cent tax on taxable income up to $6,000. A person with a taxable income of $6,000 pays just as much as members of parliament who make $18,000 a year. He also pays as much as a person who is the president of a huge corporation and makes $50,000, $60,000 or $100,000 a year. This is a regressive tax, and it is especially so in light of the poverty in Canada, with western farmers merely subsisting in many cases. This is something that should not be happening in today's society.
As a matter of fact, I believe this tax represents the Robin Hood theory in reverse, when we take money from the lower and middle income classes in this way. It is a very regressive tax and should be removed immediately.
What is social development? We have to develop our country in many ways socially, but we should not do it by imposing a tax upon the people in the lower and middle income groups. We should do it by providing these people with opportunities to improve their lot, to escape from poverty, and by giving them cultural and academic opportunities. We are not doing that.
I often ask what the priorities of the government are. What are they? Are they human priorities or are they materialistic priorities? The Minister of Finance, for example, brought down a budget last night and forecast a surplus of $250 million. In view of that fact he should have removed this tax. If he did not want to do that he could have done many other things. He could have helped the

western farmers through some kind of an emergency plan. He could have invested some of this money in some of the economically depressed areas of the country. But this was not done.
With regard to reform of the tax system, I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way made a number of comments on this matter earlier this afternoon. We must have radical reforms in the taxation system. Today, in many cases we have essentially a system of socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor. Huge corporations and many of the rich people, through various ways and means, are getting off without paying their fair share to their country. After all, in a democracy, all the people should contribute as much as they possibly can for the betterment of one another.
I know that in my own constituency of Yorkton-Melville, for example, there are many people who cannot afford to pay an extra $120 in so-called social development tax. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was right in calling it a social deception tax because these people cannot afford to pay it. They are confronted with an agricultural crisis. Many of our people are on old age pensions. Many of them are workers in unskilled jobs who just cannot afford to pay this tax while other people with higher incomes get away at a much lower rate.
As I said in the beginning, this is most indicative of the type of government we have today. I think it is basically a small "c" conservative government. It is a government that is forcing the low and middle income people to make many sacrifices because the members of the government are afraid to stick out their necks and ask for money from the huge corporations and the millionaires in this country.
There is a great need to implement many socio-economic reforms in this country, and we cannot afford to take regressive steps like this tax. We cannot afford to do so because the people are not going to put up with this kind of thing forever. The people are naturally going to rebel; they are naturally going to become very frustrated and lose more and more of their faith in the government. We
